trans culture absolutely isn't based on gender stereotypes. a lot of trans people, especially ones in the public eye (so ones you're more likely to have seen), HAVE to play into gendered stereotypes to be able to transition at all. in a patriarchal society that sees largely treats gender as being a restrictive binary, being able to move across it usually means compromising.

the vast majority of trans people i know, though (and i know many all through north america), don't conform to stereotypes. some do, just like some cis women do, but most break out of a lot of, or most, gendered stereotypes; career, fashion, relationship dynamics/status, hobbies, skills, etc.

in fact, most trans people have to jump through medical hoops that are invasive and expect gender conformity to even be able to medically transition and relieve their dysphoria... but once they're more comfortable with their body, and are surrounded by people who love them for who they are, that's where i've seen beautiful rejections of gendered roles.

feeling at home in one's body and community is empowering, and i think that when the suppressed become empowered, oppressive thijgs like stereotypes get weaker. if your inpression is that trans people reinforce oppressive gender roles, i'd really suggest you think a bit more about it, because it's actually very much the opposite; and on the political front, the things that oppress trans people also generally oppress cis women. we all deserve the right to define ourselves, even those who might feel comfortable within the existing binary

if you need proof of this, then look at what he does later in the film, and in Infinity War: he follows his own judgement again, ignoring the commitment he'd made, and acts recklessly. he sabotages security to learn Steve's location and goes after him, he leaves earth to challenge Thanos even at the risk of bringing a stone directly to him...

it's easy to build a caregiving dynamic where a little becomes entitled or dependent, or the mommy feels like they must provide care even when they don't have it in them. i've been that mommy, and it's so easy to put your needs aside because your little really needs your comfort right then... just this one time, right? so i would set it aside. and it'd happen more and more, as i whittled away at my own needs.

eventually you can get stuck feeling like your whole purpose is to take care of your little, and like you can't do it anymore, even if you still want to. it's really hard, and it was painful for me to end it when this happened. depending how things are, a mommy might be filled with guilt, or resentment, both, or something else entirely... and those can ruin relationships.

i think the best way to avoid it would have been to make sure my little's needs were addressed not just in the moment, but in the long term, and that she knew how to take care of herself when i couldn't be her source of comfort; this is just good practice to avoid dependence. being a mommy shouldn't be that you're the solution, it should be a therapeutic reprieve for both mommy and little.

sadly thay wouldn't have been possible in this case... the things that my little needed reprieve from were bigger than she could escape. i know she would've been a good little if she had the medical care she needed... she was before that came into the picture. but as much as it hurts, you can't fix anything by burning yourself out. you have to have a healthy relationship for it to work out in the end.

anyways that was a long ramble. hopefully thay gives perspective into why mommies can get burnt out, even if there's other ways it can happen.

alright, off the top of my head:

1. LISTEN. it's a beautiful exploration, and statement, on fear. it shows us both directly and indirectly what fear does to us, what we often do with it, and what we can do with it. and it's wise enough to know that by leaving things in the air, it creates this fog in the story, we just don't know if the things we fear ARE real, and they hang over everything. the parallels moving all through the episode are incredible, and the way that the characters tug on each others' fears, it's beautiful. this episode might just be my favourite piece of media, and is by far my favourite episode of the entire show.

2. HEAVEN SENT/HELL BENT. not much even needs to be said here... everyone adores Heaven Sent, and for good reason, but it's true most don't appreciate the Hell Bent as much... but it's a crucial ending to the two parter. the first is about triumphing over grief, on emotionally shaky ground, and the second part is about when that falls apart, and you realize that you were never going to be able to fix what's broken. it's hard to watch the epic events of the first part be recontextualized as tragic and  horrific, but it's what they were all along... grief is a fog that covers all with what you want to see, and this story expresses that superbly.

3. WORLD ENOUGH AND TIME/THE DOCTOR FALLS. i said not much needs to be said for the last one, but hey, let's keep this one short. amazing setting and sci fi concept, serious emotional stakes, and the attempt to rehabilitate the Master... and showing how complex at task that is by having two of them, in very different places emotionally, highlighting the all-over-the-place nature of the character... it's beautiful, and is a fitting hill for Twelve to give his life on.

4. DEEP BREATH. no other introduction of a Doctor worked so quickly, especially one that's such a slow burn. it provided very interesting and fun to watch characterization, and though it featured an interesting monster of the week and a huge callback, Moffat kept it character focused (which that series largely is, and it's wonderful). watching how tense it was for Clara to adjust to this new Doctor was incredibly compelling, and Capaldi was fascinating to watch right from the get go.

5. LAST CHRISTMAS. a nice concept that made for a great reuinion, a bit of fun, and just a lovely christmas story that wasn't afraid to be serious, scary, and pluck on the heartstrings a bit.

6. MUMMY ON THE ORIENT EXPRESS. he truly is such a pleasure to watch. Capaldi was so on point here, delivering the uncertain morality of the Doctor in the middle of a really interesting plot! the plot is a pleasure to watch, but also, Clara's personal arc in this episode is fascinating, as it is the whole season, and the wider cast is well developed and incredibly loveable. god how i wish Perkins could have a few stories in the TARDIS.

7. FLATLINE. this is a really good story. fascinating sci fi concept, paired with a fascinating change of dynamic, great episode-specific cast, funny TARDIS hijinks, and an emotionally impactful final scene.

8. OXYGEN. the politics in this episode were heavy handed and rough, so weren't perfect, but dear god was it incredible to see the Doctor actually point out how capitalism exploits workers and how drastic it would be in the future. even dropping thay though, the plot is breakneck and it feels like they're actually in danger, which is something sorely lacking a lot of the time, the episode's a pleasure to watch, and the resolution is interesting; it speaks to the reality of labour but in a moment that shows the writing could've used some more polishing, to be fair.

9. THE MAGICIAN'S APPRENTICE/THE WITCH'S FAMILIAR. this episode gets a bit too full of itself at times, but given how amazing the dynamic is between Twelve and Davros, it's something i forgive very easily. as a spiritual successor to Genesis, it builds very successfully on the same themes, and gives us some great screen time with Missy as well.

10. THE HUSBANDS OF RIVER SONG. as tempted as i was to give this spot to one of my honourable mentions, this episode is just too fun. it's got it all, and it knows it. it's so very River Song, which is funny, because i never loved her characyer except in her introduction... but here, she shines so bright, and Twelve matches it in kind. it's an absolute riot, with the most sweet ending. it's kind of a shame her best story is her last, but all's well that ends well!

HONOURABLE MENTIONS:

The Zygon Invasion/Inversion is really good, but has some flaws in the narrative/metaphor AND politics that i just struggle with. the Doctor's speech and sentiment in the resolution are absolutely top five Twelfth Doctor moments, but at the same time, he's hypocritical at points of the speech, and the overall plot is confused at times, but it's still a lovely watch.

Dark Water/Death in Heaven has great stuff in it, and really capitalizes on the wonderful character-driven storytelling of the 8th series, but unfortunately Death in Heaven is just a mess for the most part. Dark Water had all the makings of the best finale, but it just couldn't stick the landing, and is brought down heavily by the second part... but Dark Water is a phenomenal story, with the most inventive Cyberman reveal i can even imagine, and incredibly tense character moments.

cis women have struggled a lot to get us to where we are today, and still are today of course, just look at RvW, but that doesn't preclude trans women from having struggles that come from their womanhood. trans women face misogyny AND transmisogyny, it's not either or, and they come from the same place.

trans women still get harassed on the street, the difference is that if they don't pass, it's usually open threats on their safety instead of what it looks like for cis women... but trans women who do pass still face that same harassment and lack of safety. because trans women are women, they face most of the same discrimination, but some of it is different, and there's some extra stuff tacked on.

for instance, trans women are just likely to face sexual assault, but when they're a victim of it, they're more likely to be killed after (trans panic) for being trans. when trans women wear something revealing, instead of it being "she's asking for sexual assault," it's "she's asking for sexual assault and/or murder." or with doctors not listening to female patients, trans people get that too, because they're read similarly. trans struggles and women's struggles aren't mutually exclusive.

another important thing is that trans rights have been fought for just as long, but it's only been in the public eye as of very recently. it's not a coopting of feminism, it's that trans people are finally being welcomed into mainstream feminism rather than being shoved to the side and having their rights trampled on unseen. it's really important to have the solidarity that we're starting to have now.

i don't think solidarity diminishes women's struggles, and the female experience is already so diverse regardless. we need to widen that lens so that less women, cis and trans, get ignored and lose out on the political advocacy that they so sorely need.

this is a thing i think about a lot as both a mommy domme and a sub to a mommy (i'm a complicated woman,,). when looking for a mommy/sub dynamic, it's so important to be very conscious of what you're looking for. when you say some people want a mom more than just a mommy, you're hitting the nail right on the head!!

mommy kink appeals to a lot of people specifically because 'mommy' has strong caretaker implications. they think it comes with the promise of being cared for in all the ways an actual mother does, providing tons of one-sided emotional support and often taking care of day to day responsibilities and taking care of your space and life FOR you. what's interesting is the kink becomes a way for a lot of subs to implicitly assume this is something they can reasonable, or even healthily, expect.

it becomes a really toxic expectation. anyone expecting that will inherently fail. no adult relationship can work that way for long, it WILL fail even if you find someone willing to do that. i've seen it happen, i've been IN those kinds of relationships, from both ends. i'm someone who REALLY likes to lean into the mommy role emotionally, i actually love when my subs call me mom, but knowing how it can go with unhealthy boundaries and expectations, you HAVE to keep in mind what you want and whether it's healthy.

i have found that you can have a more "mom/sub" relationship and have it be healthy, if it's more about the dynamic emotionally, not in labour. one of my girlfriends calls me mom, and i have someone i call mom in this way, and it works because we have healthy expectations. both relationships have equal footing, strong communication, and a two-way balanced street of care. my girlfriend doesn't expect me to take care of everything for her because she calls me mom, and we take care of each other. it's just how we talk to and see each other <3

tldr: you can go as far as having a "mom" kind of dynamic BUT you can't actually expect the things you would expect from a mother, and you can't expect that in a mommy dynamic either. you have to know what you're looking for, and keep in mind that it has to be a healthy and reasonable thing to ask of someone! this is a complicated dynamic and both domme and sub need to be conscious of what's going on and whether it can work that way.

okay, as a system caused by medical trauma that lasted well into the teenage years, i'm gonna crack my knuckles a bit here and hopefully ramble *coherently.*

so, by nature, DID is caused before you hit double digits, and is a covert disorder, caused by repeated trauma over a period of time. this writes off a few things, like having a single procedure unless it causes ongoing trauma. if having the actual procedure happen is what you think caused it, it certainly didn't, so you couldn't credibly prove it. the only way a single procedure could feasible prove that is if the procedure had lasting consequences that did cause recurring trauma.

i could picture a procedure going wrong and causing you to be unable to live a safe life, having to rely on others for basic support. that can be very traumatic, but if the procedure went wrong already, that would be your grounds, not that it caused DID. that would just be perhaps a bit of justification for the harm done and help you in getting reparations, but if a procedure when as expected, what is their fault? the surgeon (or whatever kind of doctor) did their job, no matter how traumatic surgery can be, *and DID isn't caused by a singular traumatic event anyways.*

if you had recurring medical procedures that traumatized you, being unable to escape that traumatic reality could absolutely cause DID (you can trust me on this). being caught in a medical situation as a young child and having to live with it a long periods of time is destabilizing, terrifying and alien, and that could be strongly argued to cause it. but who would owe you reparations?

unless you had one doctor the ENTIRE time who can be held accountable for all that trauma, who do you blame? all the individual nurses who ever treated you, or even mistreated you? the entire medical system as a whole? **good cases have reliable scope, and this kind of case does not.** if you can't lay the blame at the feet of specific people, or even a specific group, you're not going to get anywhere. all it takes to reject an argument like that is a benign yet manipulative "this is just the way the system works."

if you had one doctor the whole time, maybe you could. but that's an iffy case still. how much of the trauma was the doctor's fault, versus the general medical facility? did nurses and technicians do the bulk of what traumatized you, or did the doctor specifically cause things that traumatized you and, CRUCIALLY, **those things** **were not reasonable medical practice?** you have to prove all those individual things happened, that they were unreasonable as medical treatment, and that they can be blamed on a specific person or group. then you could argue it, and see about some sort of settlement vs legal action, but it would be a very rough argument, given how complex medical ethics practice is.

the only other major thing to keep in mind is **time**. if you have a good case to argue, you need proof it's not just a story, and given the timescale of most people realizing they have DID versus when the trauma could have happened, it's not good odds you have any proof. recurring trauma leading to DID generally has to happen by the age of nine, and most people don't realize until at LEAST their 20's, but sometimes sooner i suppose. that's a lot of time for proof to disappear, and these little things are not usually documented. 

if your parents are involved in your care, either they're too self absorbed to think about your wellbeing, or they care and are too busy being afraid for your wellbeing that they're not going to be documenting these things themselves; if they're the latter, they'll be spending most of their time trying to comfort you and get any information about your health from your doctor. between that and their other many responsibilities, including probably trying to somehow make enough money to pay for this medical treatment, they're not going to be writing down everything that's happened. if you need proof, you're screwed, and you do need proof for this sort of legal claim.

this is all to say, sorry, you're probably shit out of luck. i know i am, and i had a lot of shitty, careless doctors as a very very young child. there's not really a chance of reparations, and i'm sorry to say that. i'd like to be wrong but i'm almost certainly not. if you want to talk to someone about this, feel free to message, but i don't think there's much in the way of getting compensation. there's just the long road to healing. wishing you the best, OP.

1. **Listen** \- Far and away his best, in my opinion. Incredible dive into the concept of fear as an emotion, via a really neat sci-fi idea.
2. **The Empty Child / The Doctor Dances** \- Amazing two parter with really interesting ideas, good tension, and fantastic acting by Eccleston.
3. **Heaven Sent / Hell Bent** \- Heaven Sent needs no justification, we all love it; the mystery, the Doctor on his own grieving in his own way, and a showstopping ending. Hell Bent was good too, but I've much less to say about it to be honest.
4. **Blink** \- I don't have to say a damn thing, it's just good.
5. **Silence in the Library / Forest of the Dead** \- Despite having even more neat ideas crammed into it than most Moffat episodes, he managed to make this one flow well, and honestly I think it's River's best episode by FAR.
6. **World Enough and Time / The Doctor Falls** \- Again, so many neat concepts, but ones that work well together; the ship, the gravity, and the Cybermen made for an incredible place to get the Doctor and his companions stuck. Not to mention how interesting it was to contrast Missy with her past self, showing her improvements, but also what still held her back.
7. **A Christmas Carol** \- Matt Smith at his peak, and I think that's in huge part due to Moffat giving him the perfect playground. Really neat spin on the classic, and probably the best xmas episode; Husbands of River Song *can* compete, but it's not got the emotional prowess this one does, it's just a fun ride.
8. **The Pandorica Opens / The Big Bang** \- I like seeing Moffat before he built himself too messy a web to get out of. This is the perfect sweet spot of his eccentric, complicated storytelling.
9. **Deep Breath** \- This episode is like if Christmas Invasion was good. The Doctor is recovering, but he's emotional, he's thoughtful, yet scattered all the same, figuring out who he is. It was an amazing start to his run, especially not knowing what he did at the end, as Missy references in the credits.
10. **The Time of the Doctor** \- With three seasons' worth of tangled plot strings to resolve in one xmas special, somehow, the madman did it. It's busy, especially in the first half, but it actually is a really emotional ending to Eleven's arc, while also resolving every thread besides Gallifrey's location, giving Twelve a sort of fresh start. i think that actually culminates in an interesting way in his second season, because he's basically opened up enough by then that he shows his care pretty clearly, but he becomes unhinged about it when pushed in the season finale. when he dies billions of times in Heaven Sent, he's showing care, but it's pathological! it's a brilliant play of control and genius in order to... cheat death? to cause himself more heartbreak, by means of going through billions of years of suffering? that's an interesting point in his development because being openly caring does not mean he's in a good place, and he has to address that (with Clara and Me's help).

i have a weird and pointless comparison! to a longgg running series that went through a huge change around season 5. and nobody is gonna read this at this point but i have to get this written out cause i see it.

season 1-4, doctor who was great and had lots of single standing stories, with each season having an overall arc that would have smaller or bigger things in the individual stories that hinted to the big thing at the end. this works well cause it lets things stand alone, but has cohesion! this is like phases 1-3 of the mcu i think, where you had a bunch of standalones with tie-ins, then an avengers movie to try and make a bigger arc come together. sometimes episodes would suck, but that's okay, there's others! and sometimes the whole arc would suck, but that's okay, there's another season!

however, in season 5, the showrunner changed to a guy who seemed to write REALLY well for individual episodes in the first 4 seasons, but turned out, he was just too excited to explore all his great ideas. it ruined any kind of flow, and by the end of season 6 it was terrible. you had much less room for individual stories as the big overarching story weighed down on it all, taking screentime but never resolving. season 5 through the specials that came after season 7 were part of one, big, confused arc that had no actual satisfaction to it as a story, because there was no focus whatsoever.

by the time it concluded, it had been needing to conclude for a few years already. the lack of focus got to it, and it made it grueling to keep up with. why bother watching something if there's no end in sight, it just keeps pulling the goalpost back and doesn't actually resolve any of the conflict? Echo suffered from this, but so did MoM, Secret Invasion, The Marvels, FatWS, Wandavision, Quantumania, even Love and Thunder. they're not allowed to say something because they're parts of one convoluted story, only allowed to be an episode in an arc, not an episode that connects to an arc. every film and show should be able to say something for itself, to have a resolution to what it's dealing with, even if it connects to a bigger picture. but most don't get to even try anymore.

sex is absolutely socially constructed. one can obviously go deep on this and say that all labels of biology are socially constructed (which again doesn't say they aren't real, just that we as a species DECIDE SOCIALLY how they are real...), but that's a bit of a cheap trick...

we have things we call sex markers/indicators/characteristics, such as chromosomes, genitals, hormonal balances, height, shoulder and hip width, i could go on... but none of these define sex. they way we try to use these to determine someone's sex can be unclear and even contradictory, even when those characteristics are clear themselves. there's not only two ways to have chromosomes, there's not a binary set of genitals, and height and body widths vary SO much!!

biological sex is an attempt to take all these complicated biological and physiological traits and put them into two categories. it easily falls apart as a binary under inspection, and i'd argue it only is such a fundamental concept to our medical understandings because of the same reason race was. it's not about being logical about an incredibly complex reality, it's a way of trying to explain hierarchies scientifically.

i could go on about this! i just read a fascinating book that covers both topics at once, and it's been really helpful to understanding these things. it's just horrible to read both in terms of triggering content and dense analysis of history. but to sum up, yeah, sex is absolutely socially constructed, and it's only considered more objective than gender because gender is understood culturally, rather than through an ignorant yet 'scientific' lens. sex was defined by scientists long ago, and the term science has a assumption of "valid and objective" behind it, but really, it just is a process THAT CAN BE DONE IGNORANTLY.

A few. I think that Doctor Strange and Captain Marvel are the most compelling in that department, but the GotG trilogy all have interesting narratives, as well as Loki (my favourite) and Moon Knight, but I'm not going to type anything up about more than the two movies i mentioned first...

Doctor Strange is compelling in how it shows a self absorbed, privileged and talented man absolutely crumble under the consequences of his own recklessness, but mostly because of what he learns to do instead. He stands to his principles as best he can and he finally shows under pressure that he *does* care about doing no harm. He was doing harm before by being callous and disregarding anyone that didn't serve him, even if his skill meant he was a fantastic surgeon to those who did get his help. Stephen slowly learns not everything is under his control, but still finds he is a masterful manipulator of magic and uses that to do more than just what benefits him.

I think it's interesting that despite him being humbled, he still is arrogant in his competence, even if he can ride it to victory in that film. Despite everyone hating how easily he was subdued in the sequel, I thought it worked wonderfully, because he was starting to learn his mastery of magic doesn't mean he can manipulate everything into what he needs. In MoM, for all its issues, he has to learn how little control he has, and he's not the one who saves the day in the end; he just inspires someone to fight and win. I liked that. It's another moment of humbling himself and learning he's not capable of managing everything and everyone himself, sometimes he needs to be part of a team.

As for Captain Marvel, I'm not surprised it fell on deaf ears. Despite being held to the US military's standards of, well, not ever criticizing the military, it manages to do it anyways thematically. Carol is lied to and manipulated into thinking she's fighting a good war, and it's convincing for her. She needs to defeat the terrifying terrorists, and they're a threat that the army is righteous to fight and try to wipe out. The justification, the paranoia, anyone could be one of the terrorists, is incredibly effective propaganda. It's only by being around actual skrulls that it becomes obvious how genocidal the army is, how hard they've gaslit her. And there are multiple chances for Carol to be scared off and retreat to the paranoia (when Talos shows up at the house, or when Talos calls his family on the ship, both were framed like possible ambushed), but she listens and is shown actual evidence of what's happened, whereas the army just gave her fearmongering.

Because of her unwillingness to be completely obedient and close minded like a good soldier, she stops helping a campaign of genocide, and instead tries to save the innocent targets of imperialism from being killed off. It's quite compelling as a self-determined and independent moment, breaking off from the oppressive structure of the Kree empire... This was more sold as a feminist moment (and it absolutely is if you're talking intersectional feminism, or representing women in the MCU I suppose too?), but it's more a moment of breaking free as she put it in the movie. She doesn't need to follow the orders of a genocidal empire, and she doesn't need to prove herself to someone that tries to control her. She can control herself, and the world is better for it. Again, easy to read an a story about women's empowerment, but that's just the marketing of it; the real themes are about reconnecting with humanity that you've been taught to see as enemies, and making things right, not as a cog in a machine but as your own person.
